metadata.document: Environmental Defence Society submission on the Planning Bill and the Natural Environment Bill

cleaned_body_text: Environmental Defence Society submission on the Planning Bill and the Natural Environment Bill SUBMITTER DETAILS FULL NAME: Environmental Defence Society Incorporated ADDRESS FOR SERVICE: PO Box 91736, Victoria Street West, Auckland 1142 CONTACT: Greg Severinsen, Shay Schlaepfer EMAIL: greg@eds.org.nz and shay@eds.org.nz Introduction 1. The Environmental Defence Society (EDS) thanks the Environment Select Committee for the opportunity to make a submission on the Planning Bill and the Natural Environment Bill (NEB) (collectively, the Bills). On 3 February 2026 the Committee authorised a 1-week extension for EDS to lodge its submission by 4:30pm on 20 February 2026. 2. EDS is an apolitical, not-for-profit organisation dedicated to achieving improved environmental outcomes for all New Zealanders. It is active as a litigator, policy think tank, events convenor and environmental advocate. It has dedicated considerable resource over the past seven years into looking at the future of the resource management system in Aotearoa New Zealand. 3. In particular, over the course of 2024-2025 EDS did an in-depth piece of work looking at the very issues that the Bills are seeking to address. The project’s final report of September 2025, entitled Replacing the Resource Management Act – Risks and solutions, can be found on EDS’s website. Among other things, it explored regulatory relief, environmental limits, spatial planning, standardisation, public participation and scope. It also involved detailed comparison with international jurisdictions, including the United Kingdom, Ireland, Singapore and Australia. This work has informed EDS’s submission on the Bills. 4. EDS opposes the Bills in their present form. Significant changes are needed to make them acceptable and workable. 5. However, we do not consider this to be fatal to the passage of the Bills. The Resource Management Act 1991 (RMA), which the Bills are designed to replace, is not fit for purpose and requires either replacement or fundamental amendment. The Bills could achieve that outcome if amended as recommended in this submission. Preliminary comments 6. Although the Bills are being described as the largest ‘economic’ reforms in a generation, they should not be, at their heart, about the economy. They should be about protecting, managing and restoring the environment. This needs to be the lens through which the reforms are assessed. 7. Looking through this lens does not prevent consideration of how to make the system more enabling, efficient, certain and user-friendly. That is necessary, given deficiencies in the RMA. Nor does it prevent efforts to grow the economy within proper environmental constraints. However, we do not have an economy – or healthy society – without the natural world on which our survival and wellbeing depend. It should be the cornerstone of any good environmental law. 8. Our natural environment is currently in bad shape. It requires not just protection but also improvement. For example, we have the highest proportion of threatened or at-risk indigenous species in the world, more than half of our rare ecosystems are at risk of collapse, ninety percent of wetlands have been lost since pre-human settlement, forty six percent of groundwater monitoring sites failed to meet drinking water standards for E.coli at least once between 2019 and 2024, and between 2016 and 2020, 55 percent of groundwater monitoring sites suffered from moderate or severe organic pollution. 9. In this submission we describe the ways in which the Bills need to change. 10. We have provided or described specific drafting changes where appropriate, which are collated in the Appendix attached to this submission. Tracked changes have been used where possible. 11. Because the two Bills are so interlinked (there are many cross-references, sharing of legislative machinery, and other relationships), our submission is structured according to topics that frequently cut across them, rather than dealing with each Bill in turn. 12. Most important are the provisions concerning regulatory relief, environmental limits, and standing and public participation. 13. While these three topics are of most concern and comprise the bulk of our submission, there are other elements of the Bills (including their scope) that require change. 14. There are also many positive aspects of the Bills that should be retained and built upon or strengthened. Our submission highlights a number of these where they relate to the themes we discuss. 15. However, in addition to the specific issues we raise in this submission, there are more general themes that run through multiple topics that are of concern. 16. The pervasive and cross-cutting nature of these themes points to a need to slow down resource management reforms, integrate them with other policy processes and undertake a global assessment of the whole package. 17. EDS encourages the Committee to closely consider the submissions of tangata whenua with respect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Regulatory relief Introduction 18. The most egregious aspect of the Bills is the regulatory relief framework, which will require compensation where certain kinds of public interest environmental or planning regulation impacts the use of private land. 19. There are two separate regulatory relief pathways proposed in the Bills. The first is completely new and applies to things called ‘specified rules’. This pathway is unacceptable and needs to be deleted from the Bills. 20. The second is much broader, because it applies to all ‘provisions’ in plans. Essentially, it is a modified version of section 85 of the RMA. An analogous provision should remain in both the NEB and Planning Bill, but in quite a different form. 21. For the reasons set out below, as currently proposed, the regulatory relief pathways are likely to result in planning chaos. Philosophical foundation for regulatory relief 22. The Bills’ regulatory relief frameworks are premised on a philosophical ideology that people should be able to do what they want with their land. Pathway 1: Regulatory relief for specified rules 27. A relief framework must be included in a ‘proposed land use plan’ and/or a ‘natural environment plan’ prior to notification if it is ‘reasonably likely’ that a specified rule will have a ‘significant impact’ on the ‘reasonable use’ of land. 64. Both pathways for relief are likely to have a significant chilling effect on legitimate public interest environmental regulation. Summary of solutions required for regulatory relief 96. The only meaningful solution to the deep problems with the specified rules relief pathway is to remove it entirely. Environmental limits 98. It is positive that the NEB provides for environmental limits, given that the RMA is deficient in that regard. Public participation and legal standing 244. Both Bills excessively constrain the ability of the public and environmental groups to be involved in decision-making on plans and consents. Scope 280. The scope of the Bills to control environmental effects has been narrowed considerably, and excessively, compared to the RMA. Issues in the marine environment 297. Many of the more general concerns outlined in this submission apply to decision-making in the marine environment. Split legislation 323. Splitting the RMA into separate legislation for the natural environment and land use creates problems, overlaps and procedural complexities. Restrictions 334. The restrictions currently contained in Part 3 of the RMA are largely left unchanged under the Bills. Procedural principles and timeframes 338. We support the inclusion of a precautionary principle in cl 166 of the NEB, where consent authorities are obliged to favour caution and environmental protection where there is uncertainty in information. Effects thresholds 345. Under cl 15(1)(b) of the NEB, decision-makers must not consider a less than minor adverse effect unless the cumulative effect of 2 or more such effects create effects that are greater than less than minor. Water conservation orders 350. EDS supports the retention of existing water conservation orders under cl 23 of Schedule 1 of the Planning Bill. Interaction with other legislation 357. Neither the NEB nor the Planning Bill refer to the Waitakere Ranges Heritage Area Act (WRHAA). Transition 372. Our primary concern about the transition between the RMA and the new system is how environmental limits are provided for. Compliance monitoring and enforcement 382. EDS generally supports the strengthening of compliance and enforcement tools in the Bills. Concluding remarks 383. Although there is a pressing need to replace the RMA, as drafted the Bills will be a step backwards.
